primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Neutralizing IgG autoantibodies against GM-CSF impair GM-CSF-dependent maturation and function of alveolar macrophages. The macrophages cannot adequately catabolize and clear surfactant from the alveolar surface, so lipoproteinaceous surfactant accumulates within alveoli and impairs gas exchange.
vignette: A 39-year-old man has several months of progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. High-resolution CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with superimposed interlobular and intralobular septal thickening. Bronchoalveolar lavage returns opaque, milky fluid containing foamy macrophages and abundant amorphous material that stains strongly with periodic acid-Schiff. Serum testing detects high-titer IgG antibodies against GM-CSF.
lead: Which cellular abnormality most directly causes the accumulation of material in this patient’s alveoli?
correct: Impaired GM-CSF-dependent clearance of surfactant by alveolar macrophages
distractors: Excess synthesis and secretion of surfactant by hyperactive type II pneumocytes
Failure of axonemal dynein in respiratory epithelial cilia, reducing mucociliary transport
Defective NADPH oxidase activity in phagocytes, preventing the respiratory burst
Increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure causing transudation of protein-poor fluid into alveoli
distractor_notes: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis reflects decreased clearance of surfactant rather than increased production. Type II pneumocyte hypersecretion is not the mechanism of autoimmune PAP.

Axonemal dynein defects cause primary ciliary dyskinesia with impaired mucociliary clearance, recurrent sinopulmonary infection, and laterality abnormalities; they do not produce PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous alveolar filling.

NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease and impaired killing of catalase-positive organisms. Autoimmune PAP instead reflects dysfunctional alveolar macrophages from loss of effective GM-CSF signaling.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema can produce diffuse opacities and hypoxemia, but hydrostatic fluid is not the PAS-positive surfactant-rich material and anti-GM-CSF antibodies identify a different mechanism.
key_expl: This is autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. Neutralizing anti-GM-CSF antibodies block GM-CSF signaling that is required for normal alveolar macrophage differentiation and function. The macrophages become unable to clear and catabolize surfactant efficiently, causing surfactant-rich lipoproteinaceous material to accumulate in the alveoli. This produces impaired diffusion/gas exchange, a characteristic ground-glass plus septal-thickening ('crazy-paving') pattern, and milky bronchoalveolar lavage containing PAS-positive material. The disorder is caused by defective clearance rather than increased surfactant production.
objective: Explain autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis as a GM-CSF autoantibody-mediated defect in alveolar macrophage surfactant clearance.
